2027-06-13.title: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles

Trust in the providence of God
2027-06-13.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 1:33–2:1, 1 Corinthians 14:1–19 and Luke 12:16–34 (with the parable of the rich fool).
2027-06-13.verse: “Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
theo: On this Fifth Sunday of the Apostles the readings set before us two ways of facing the future: fear and trust. The first reading takes us to Kadesh, on the southern edge of the promised land. Moses reminds the people of the day when the spies came back from Canaan with fruit in their hands and fear in their hearts. The land was good, but its cities were walled and its people tall, and Israel refused to go up. Moses had pleaded with them: the Lord your God “goes before you on the way to seek out a place for you to camp, in fire by night, and in the cloud by day, to show you the route you should take.” They had seen the sea divided and the manna fall, yet they would not trust. So the Lord said that this generation would not see the good land, “except Caleb son of Jephunneh,” because of “his complete fidelity to the Lord.” Then came the second mistake, the mirror image of the first. Having refused to go when God said go, the people now insisted on going when God said stay: “We have sinned against the Lord! We are ready to go up and fight.” The Lord warned them: “Do not go up and do not fight, for I am not in the midst of you.” They went anyway, and the Amorites “chased you as bees do.” Fear refuses to move with God; presumption rushes ahead without him. Both are failures of the same thing, which is trust. And notice the tender detail in the middle of the judgment: the little ones, whom the frightened parents expected to become booty, are the very ones who will enter the land. God's promise was never withdrawn; it passed to the next generation.

Isaiah's oracle is a lament over Jerusalem, “the faithful city,” which has become unfaithful like a wife who has betrayed her husband. Strong language, but the charge is specific. The city's silver “has become dross,” its wine “is mixed with water.” Its leaders love bribes; “they do not defend the orphan, and the widow’s cause does not come before them.” For the prophets, unfaithfulness to God shows itself first in injustice to the weak. Yet the fire Isaiah announces is the fire of a refiner, not of a destroyer: “I will smelt away your dross as with lye and remove all your alloy. And I will restore your judges as at the first, and your counselors as at the beginning. Afterward you shall be called the city of righteousness, the faithful city.” God burns away what is false in order to recover what is precious. Only those who cling to their idols, the sacred oaks and gardens of the old fertility cults, are left like “a garden without water.” In the monsoon month, when every compound in Kerala turns green and every well fills, the image speaks clearly: a soul without God is a garden in which the rain has stopped.

Paul writes to a lively and gifted Church in Corinth, where some prized the gift of tongues above everything. He does not despise any gift of the Spirit, but he gives them an order: “Pursue love and strive for the spiritual gifts, and especially that you may prophesy.” Prophecy here means speaking God's word in a way others can understand, so that they are built up, encouraged and consoled. A gift that only edifies its owner is less than a gift that edifies the Church. Paul's examples are homely: a flute or a harp that does not give distinct notes, a bugle that “gives an indistinct sound,” so that no one knows it is time to prepare for battle. “So with yourselves; since you are eager for spiritual gifts, strive to excel in them for building up the church.” In this Season of the Apostles, when we thank God for the Spirit given at Pentecost, Paul reminds every prayer group, every choir, every catechist and every preacher of the test: does what I do build up the Church in love? A clear word spoken kindly in a family is worth more than an impressive word that leaves everyone confused.

In the Gospel Jesus turns to his disciples and speaks the words that have comforted anxious people ever since: “do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will wear.” He points to the ravens, birds that the Law counted unclean and that no farmer ever fed: “they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them. Of how much more value are you than the birds!” He points to the lilies, which “neither toil nor spin; yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like one of these.” Worry adds nothing: “can any of you by worrying add a single hour to your span of life?” Jesus does not forbid work or planning; the birds hunt and the lilies grow. What he forbids is the anxious grasping that makes us forget the Father. “Instead, strive for his kingdom, and these things will be given to you as well.” Then comes the tenderest sentence of the passage: “Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.” The apostles were a little flock indeed, a handful of fishermen and tax collectors. The Church in India has often been a little flock too, from the first communities that tradition traces to Mar Thoma. The kingdom is not something we must seize; it is the Father's pleasure to give it. Therefore the disciple can be generous: “Sell your possessions, and give alms. Make purses for yourselves that do not wear out.” The longer form of the Gospel adds the rich man who planned bigger barns and heard, “You fool! This very night your life is being demanded of you.” The Kadesh generation, the faithless city and the rich fool all made the same mistake: they trusted in what they could see. Jesus ends with a question for every heart: “For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
conn: Fire by night and cloud by day.
“The Lord went in front of them in a pillar of cloud by day, to lead them along the way, and in a pillar of fire by night, to give them light” (Exodus 13:21).
“But my servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit and has followed me wholeheartedly, I will bring into the land” (Numbers 14:24).
The Letter to the Hebrews reads the story of Kadesh as a warning: “So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:19).
Of the coming Lord Malachi says: “he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver” (Malachi 3:3); faith is “more precious than gold that, though perishable, is tested by fire” (1 Peter 1:7).
“I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28), fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:17).
Matthew's form of the same teaching: “But strive first for the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well” (Matthew 6:33).
“Do not worry about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God” (Philippians 4:6).
altar: Israel was fed in the wilderness by a God who went before them in fire and cloud. At the Holy Qurbana the same Father feeds his little flock with the Bread of life, the treasure that no thief can steal and no moth destroy.
When the priest raises the Body and Blood of the Lord, he lifts our hearts with them. There, where our treasure is, our hearts are taught to stay.
outline: Two ways of facing tomorrow: fear that refuses and presumption that rushes, or the trust of a little flock.
Point 1 · The God who goes before you
Kadesh: refusing to go, then going without God; Caleb's complete fidelity; the little ones who enter.
A faithful city that forgot the orphan and the widow; God burns away dross to recover silver.
Point 3 · Pursue love, build up the Church
Gifts given for others; a bugle with a clear sound.
Point 4 · Do not be afraid, little flock
Ravens and lilies; strive for the kingdom; treasure in heaven.
A garden in the monsoon rain, and a garden where the rain has stopped.
“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
live: Name one thing you have been afraid to do although you know God is asking it, and take the first step this week.
Defend the orphan and the widow (Isaiah 1:23)
Find out about one widow, orphan or elderly person living alone in your parish ward and do something concrete for them this week.
Before you speak in a meeting, a family discussion or a WhatsApp group this week, ask: will this build up or only show off?
Each night this week write down one worry and place it before the Father in prayer; then give one alms you had not planned.
fathers: Preaching on the rich man who wanted bigger barns, Basil said: the bread you hoard belongs to the hungry, the coat in your chest to the naked, the shoes rotting in your house to the barefoot, the money you bury to the needy. The barns that hold your wealth are the stomachs of the poor.

Do you want to keep your treasure safe? Send it ahead. The poor are like porters who carry what you give into heaven, where no thief breaks in. What you keep you will leave behind; what you give goes before you.

Paul does not say simply, love; he says, pursue love, as a hunter pursues his quarry without tiring. Love is the root from which every gift draws its sap; the gift that builds up others is the one love chooses.
magis: Jesus asks for childlike abandonment to the providence of our heavenly Father, who takes care of his children's smallest needs: therefore do not be anxious, but seek first his kingdom.
Asking for our daily bread expresses filial trust; it is not passivity, but the confidence of children who know the Father gives what they need.
The Lord grieves over the rich, because they find their consolation in the abundance of goods; detachment from riches is necessary for entering the kingdom of heaven.

Charisms, extraordinary or simple and humble, are graces of the Holy Spirit that directly or indirectly benefit the Church, ordered as they are to her building up; they are to be accepted with gratitude, and charity is their true measure.
saints: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar the Eleventh Sunday in Ordinary Time; the memorial of St Antony of Padua (c. 1195–1231), the Franciscan preacher so dearly loved in Kerala, gives way to the Sunday this year.
Wed 16: in the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church the Apostles' Fast begins. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Thu 24: the Birth of John the Baptist.
2027-06-13.prayer: Lord God, you went before your people in fire by night and cloud by day, and you never withdrew your promise. Forgive us when fear has kept us from following you and when pride has made us rush ahead without you. Refine us as silver is refined, and make our homes and our parish faithful and just to the orphan and the widow. Holy Spirit, give us gifts that build up your Church, and above all give us love. Lord Jesus, teach your little flock not to be afraid, to seek the kingdom first, and to keep our treasure, and so our hearts, with you. Glory to the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.

quick: Deuteronomy: at Kadesh Israel first refused to go up in fear, then went up without God in presumption; Caleb followed the Lord wholeheartedly.
Isaiah: the faithful city forgot the orphan and the widow; God will smelt away its dross and make it again the city of righteousness.
Paul: pursue love and strive for the gifts that build up the Church.
Luke: do not worry; consider the ravens and the lilies; do not be afraid, little flock; where your treasure is, there your heart will be.
2027-06-13.action: Write down your greatest worry, give it to the Father in prayer tonight, and give one alms this week that you had not planned.
2027-06-13.question: Where is my treasure, and so where is my heart?
catechism: Charisms for building up the Church.
kidsaint: Father Chavara was a priest in Kerala more than one hundred and fifty years ago. He wanted every child, rich or poor, to learn to read and write, and he asked that a school be started beside every church. He began religious congregations of priests and of sisters, a printing press and a home for the poor, and he often had very little money for all this. He trusted that God the Father would provide, and God did. Lesson: as you go back to school this June, thank God for your school, study well, and trust your Father in heaven with your worries!
2027-06-13.special: Fifth Sunday of the Apostles. Latin calendar: Eleventh Sunday in Ordinary Time (St Antony of Padua omitted this year).
term: The litany of intercession sung or said by the deacon (or the priest) in the Holy Qurbana and in the Hours, to which the people answer with a short prayer. The word comes from the Syriac for proclamation. In the Karozutha the whole Church lays its needs before the Father, for the Church and her pastors, the sick, travellers and the departed: Jesus' teaching on not worrying becomes a prayer. Malayalam: കാറോസൂസ.

family.explain: Jesus told his friends not to worry so much about food and clothes. He said: look at the crows. They do not plant rice or keep it in a store room, but God feeds them. Look at the flowers. They do not sew dresses, but they are more beautiful than a king's robes. You are worth much more than birds and flowers! God is our Father and he knows what we need. So we work and study, but we do not worry; we pray and trust him.
family.intention: We pray for families who do not have enough food, and for children starting a new school year.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing we are worried about? Let us give it to God together now.”

illus: In a hill village in Idukki a widow ran a small tea shop to pay for her two children's education. Every June, when the schools reopened and fees, books and uniforms all fell due in the same week of heavy rain, she would lie awake counting. One year a neighbour found her at the shop at five in the morning, saying her rosary over the account book. ‘You look worried,’ he said. ‘I was,’ she answered, ‘until I remembered that I am not the father of this family; God is. My job is to do my work and keep my heart in the right place.’ That morning, as every morning, she set aside a glass of tea and a bun for an old man who slept at the bus stop. Her children both finished their studies. Her son says now: ‘We never had much money, but we never once saw our mother give up giving.’

pm.open: Father in heaven, you feed the ravens and clothe the lilies. We are your little flock, gathered in the Spirit of Pentecost. Take away our fear, build us up in love, and make our hearts rest where our treasure is, in you. Amen.
share: The Lord your God goes before you on the way (Deuteronomy 1:33). Where have I refused to follow because I was afraid?
Do not go up… for I am not in the midst of you (Deuteronomy 1:42). Where have I rushed ahead without asking God?
Strive to excel in them for building up the church (1 Corinthians 14:12). How does my gift build up others?
Do not be afraid, little flock (Luke 12:32). What worry do I need to hand over to the Father tonight?
interc: For the Church in this Season of the Apostles, that she may not be afraid to go where the Spirit leads.
For leaders in government and in the Church, that they may defend the orphan and the widow and refuse every bribe.
For all who are anxious about money, health or the future, especially parents at the start of the school year.
For prayer groups and all who have spiritual gifts, that they may use them in love to build up the Church.
For farmers and for all affected by the monsoon rains, that they may be protected and blessed.
pm.close: Father, your Son told his little flock not to be afraid, because it is your pleasure to give us the kingdom. Deliver us from fear and from presumption, refine us in your love, and keep our hearts where our treasure is. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, there are two ways to face tomorrow. One is the way of fear; the other is the way of trust. Today's readings show us both.

At Kadesh the people of Israel stood at the edge of the promised land. The land was good, but they were afraid, and they refused to go in, though the Lord had gone before them “in fire by night, and in the cloud by day” (Deuteronomy 1:33). Then, when God told them to wait, they rushed ahead without him and were defeated. Fear says, I will not go even with God. Presumption says, I will go even without God. Only Caleb followed the Lord with his whole heart.

Isaiah weeps over Jerusalem, a faithful city that has forgotten the orphan and the widow. But God's fire is the fire of a refiner: he burns away the dross to find the silver. When God allows trials in our lives, he is not destroying us; he is purifying us, so that we may again be called faithful.

Saint Paul tells the Corinthians, proud of their spiritual gifts: “Pursue love” (1 Corinthians 14:1). Every gift of the Spirit is for building up the Church. A trumpet that gives an unclear sound helps no one. Let our words and our gifts be clear and kind, for the good of others.

And Jesus says: do not worry. Look at the ravens; look at the lilies. Your Father knows what you need. “Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). The kingdom is a gift. We do not have to grab it; we have only to receive it and share it.

This June, when schools reopen and fees fall due and the rains are heavy, many of us carry worries. Let us bring them to this altar. Let us strive first for the kingdom, give generously to the poor, and keep our treasure in heaven, for where our treasure is, there our heart will be also. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus says: look at the birds. Nobody gives them a lunch box, but God feeds them. Look at the flowers. Nobody sews their clothes, but they are beautiful.
You are worth much more than birds and flowers! So when you feel worried about school or anything else, tell God your Father. He loves you and he will take care of you.

intro: Theme: “Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.”
On the Fifth Sunday of the Apostles: a people who would not trust at Kadesh, a city refined by fire, gifts given to build up the Church, and the little flock that need not fear.

So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.
points.apply: Take the first step this week in one thing God has been asking of you, and ask his guidance before every big decision.

so that the genuineness of your faith… being more precious than gold that, though perishable, is tested by fire… may be found to result in praise and glory and honor when Jesus Christ is revealed.

Love as the measure of every gift.

points.h: Do not be afraid, little flock
sub: Treasure in heaven, heart in heaven.
q: do not fear, for I am with you, do not be afraid, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my victorious right hand.
“Do not be afraid, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.
points.apply: Each night this week, hand one worry to the Father, and give one alms you had not planned.

concl: Fear and presumption both fail the test of trust; the Father who went before Israel goes before his little flock today.
Refined by his fire and built up in love, we can strive for the kingdom without anxiety, because our treasure and our heart are with him.
2027-06-13.resolve: This week, take one step of trust, help one person in need, speak only to build up, and give each worry to the Father in prayer.
